Just now

--

I need to confess something embarrassing, because I know I’m not the only one doing it.
I was building a website with Claude Code. I needed that thing where a row of client logos slides across the screen forever. You’ve seen it on a thousand landing pages. Smooth, endless, hypnotic.
I did not know what it was called. So I described it the best way I could:
“Horizontally stacked icons that animate from left to right and span the entire width of the screen.”
Fourteen words. I was proud of those fourteen words. They felt precise.
Claude built something that slid the wrong way. So I explained again, with more words. It built something that didn’t loop. More words. It built a grid that didn’t move at all. By day three I was burning credits at 2am, genuinely angry at a computer, convinced the model was broken.
Spoiler: the model was fine.

The Pinterest moment
On day four I did something I should have done on day one. Instead of describing the thing again, I took a screenshot of the design I was copying and ran a reverse image search. Pinterest answered in about one second.
It’s called a marquee.
I typed one word into Claude Code. “Add a marquee of client logos.” It nailed it instantly, first try, exactly what I’d been chasing for three days.
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Holy shit. Three days. One word.
I sat there for a minute just staring at it. Not at the marquee. At myself.

The part nobody tells vibe coders
Here’s what I realized, and it’s the reason I’m writing this instead of quietly moving on with my life.
If you’re building things with AI without a coding background, everyone sells you “prompt engineering.” Templates, role play, magic phrases. But no prompt template on earth would have saved me. My problem was never how I prompted. It was vocabulary.
Actual developers already know this trick. They don’t describe components. They name them. They scroll through component libraries the way you scroll through Netflix, and every pattern they see has a label attached. That’s half their superpower, and nobody mentions it because to them it’s completely obvious.
A name works because it’s compression. “Marquee” points to an exact concept the model already knows in full detail. My fourteen proud words were a blurry sketch of something that already had a precise address. I was describing the map when I could have given the coordinates.
And the model? It was never confused. I just didn’t speak the language yet.

The language is small
The good news is that this language is tiny. You don’t need a computer science degree. You need maybe thirty words.
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Toast: the little “Saved!” popup that disappears on its own. Skeleton loader: the grey shapes that hold the page’s place while it loads. Sticky header: the navbar that stays glued to the top. Accordion: the expanding rows in every FAQ. Bento grid: the mixed-size boxes on every modern landing page.
Each one of these names replaces a paragraph of frustrated description. Each one saves you time, credits, and at least one 2am argument with a machine.
How do you learn them? Three ways, all free. Reverse image search any design you’re copying. Scroll a component library like shadcn/ui or Material UI and just look at the pictures with their names. Or simply ask your agent “what is this pattern called?” before you ask it to build anything.
One honest caveat: this only works for things that already have names. If you’re inventing genuinely new UI, you’ll still have to describe it. But be honest, you’re probably not. Most of what we build has been built before, and someone already named it.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

Name it, don’t describe it
So the next time your agent keeps missing, stop and ask yourself which problem you actually have. Is the model failing to understand you? Or are you failing to name the thing?
For me it was the second one, three days in a row.
I put together a free field guide of the 24 UI terms I wish I knew on day one, each with a picture so you recognize it on sight, plus the exact phrase to say to your coding agent. Grab it here Ui-vocabulary-guide, and go build something.
